content:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-15
Start time: 18:30 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Eli Navarro (Redwood Solutions Eng), Priya Raman (Helmora Head of ML), James Cole (Helmora Infra), Marta Li (Helmora Product), Tom Benson (Helmora SRE)

Summary:
Quick POC sync reviewing latest KV/prefix hit-rate numbers, discussing a new "thermostat" approach to eviction (adaptive TTL/coalescing), prompt-reuse patterns observed, and next steps for staged tuning + a deeper SRE/infra session. Some background noise and minor transcription errors.

Topics covered:
- Current KV cache and prefix-reuse hit rates (staging + prod-ish sampling)
- Adaptive eviction / "thermostat" idea (auto TTL based on hit-rate/latency targets)
- Prompt normalization and reuse heuristics (token tradeoffs)
- Warmstart/session-affinity impacts and burst behavior
- Security/compliance questions (KMS, VPC, SOC2 logs)

Action items (captured above): list of owners and due dates.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. quick check — can folks hear me?
[00:10] Priya: yes good, can hear you. sorry for the late hour here.
[00:15] Samir: okay awesome. agenda: we wanted to run through the latest hit-rate exports you shared, show a small experiment we ran with an adaptive TTL "thermostat" and walk through suggested knob defaults. lena will lead the tech bits.
[00:30] Lena: hi all. quick note — some of the numbers in the sheet looked like they were sampled at different windows so i re-aligned them to 24h. i also noticed some odd prefix canonicalization differences that impact reuse.
[00:45] James: yeah we saw that — our frontend sometimes appends a trailing space in user messages, and that broke prefix matching so hit-rate looked lower.
[00:50] Eli: mhm, small normalizations go a long way, we have a couple heuristics for trimming punctuation + normalizing whitespace.
[01:20] Marta: real quick, what's the current kv hit rate again? the sheet said 37% but then there was a 29% number. which is which?
[01:30] Samir: good question — the 29% was raw across all sessions including bot traffic; after filtering human prompts and normalizing, the effective KV hit sits at about 42% on staging, 37% on mixed-prod sampling.
[01:50] Priya: that delta makes sense. what about prefix reuse specifically?
[02:00] Lena: prefix reuse — we computed canonical prefix buckets where repeated leading tokens matched, that came in around 18% effective reuse after normalization.
[02:15] Tom: 18% ok, i guess that explains some of the latency variance. what p95 token latency are you seeing on served hits vs miss?
[02:30] Lena: on hits p95 is ~42ms, misses go to ~220ms in our sampling. p50 numbers are ~15ms and ~120ms respectively. these are on the dedicated small pool we used for tests, YMMV.
[03:00] James: 220ms p95 misses — that aligns with our observed flares. cost delta per token?
[03:10] Eli: approximate token cost delta is 3.5x on misses versus hits — because misses invoke more runtime and KV lookups + no prefix caching.
[03:40] Priya: ok. so tell us about this thermostat idea — how does it differ from static TTL or eviction?
[03:50] Lena: the thermostat is basically an adaptive TTL + coalescing policy. instead of a static TTL we track per-prefix utility and adjust TTL up when reuse/hit-rate is high and bring it down when hit-rate drops or we see noise. it also has a small burst window to keep recent sessions warm if there is affinity.
[04:20] Samir: think of it like a temperature controller: target hit-rate is the set point, you adjust TTL (and optionally the eviction priority) to maintain that set point while respecting memory and latency SLOs.
[04:35] Marta: does it require extra infra? sounds like more metadata to store.
[04:45] Lena: minimal — we store per-prefix counters and a tiny EWMA. it's about kilobytes per hot prefix. the heavy lifting is in eviction policy which we're pushing into the runtime so it's parallelizable.
[05:10] James: concerns on consistency across replicas — if you have variable TTLs do all replicas converge?
[05:20] Eli: good point. we discussed two modes — local thermostat (per node) and global thermostat (coordinator). local is simpler and lower latency, global gives more consistent experience but needs small control channel. we demoed local in this POC.
[05:50] Priya: any weird regressions? did you see cases where TTL increased and caused staleness in completions?
[06:05] Lena: in content generation we saw negligible semantic staleness — the prefix is just reused to fill KV caches, outputs remain generated live. main risk is if your prompts evolve; there we recommend a decay term that drops TTL if prompt drift is detected.
[06:35] Tom: prompt drift detection — how sensitive is that? false positives could flush useful cache.
[06:45] Lena: we use cosine similarity on prefix embeddings at a cheap sampling rate; threshold tuning avoids thrash, but james needs to try on your real traffic to tune.
[07:10] James: noted. we'll add an embedding-sample run to staging.
[07:20] Priya: what about prompt normalization — is that handled in the runtime or do we do it upstream?
[07:30] Samir: both options exist. runtime normalization is safer (single place) but upstream normalization reduces neural-text variance too. we generally recommend basic normalization upstream and have runtime as a fallback.
[07:55] Marta: cost question — if we bump TTLs to raise hit-rate to say 60%, what's the memory impact?
[08:05] Eli: depends on prefix cardinality. we estimated with your workload that 60% would increase cache memory by ~28% in the small pool test, but token-cost per request drops ~22% so net cost savings are likely. we put the sample numbers in the sheet.
[08:40] Priya: interesting — so there's a sweet spot. do you help find that or we iterate?
[08:50] Samir: yes, Redwood Optimize can run a sweep for you; lena and eli can propose defaults and then we run 1-2 staged experiments.
[09:05] James: i want to understand eviction policy interaction with session affinity — some of our flows are session-heavy with long dialogues.
[09:15] Lena: for long dialogues, session-affinity keeps the session's KV hot. thermostat can add a bias to affinity sessions so TTL decays slower. we also have a session weight multiplier.
[09:40] Tom: do you support pinning model variants or routing to cheaper model on misses?
[09:50] Samir: yes that's part of the smart routing layer — fallback to cheaper quantized variant on heavy misses is supported, and we can policy-route based on cost/latency.
[10:10] Marta: any security concerns for storing these prefixes? are they encrypted or do they contain PII?
[10:20] Eli: by default we recommend hashing or tokenizing sensitive inputs before caching; runtime supports KMS integration and we log only metrics, not raw prompts. for Private deployments you can configure HSM/KMS and no plaintext leaves cluster.
[10:45] Priya: SOC2 — you have docs? our audit team will ask.
[10:50] Samir: yes we'll share our SOC2 + the data handling playbook; lena will include a short note on where prefixes are stored and retention defaults.
[11:15] James: back to measurements — what's your confidence interval on the hit-rate uplift with thermostat? i.e., how repeatable is it?
[11:25] Eli: in our internal runs on similar workloads thermostat increased effective reuse by 8–12 percentage points with p < 0.05 across 48h windows. your mileage depends on prompt shape and session churn.
[11:45] Marta: do you have a lightweight toggle/kill switch if we see negative effects?
[11:55] Lena: absolutely. we provide immediate fallback to baseline TTL plus canarying by user cohort. we recommend a 10% traffic canary first.
[12:20] Priya: can we see an example of where thermostat backfired?
[12:30] Eli: one internal example — when we had very high ephemeral noise (bots repeatedly generating random prefixes) thermostat increased TTL for junk prefixes; solved by adding quality filters and minimum reuse thresholds.
[12:55] James: ok good to know. we'll need those heuristics in the runbook.
[13:05] Samir: i'm going to share a short annotated sheet with the exact thresholds we used.
[13:15] Marta: about prompt reuse heuristics — are you deduping templates vs free text?
[13:25] Lena: yes we have template detection (regex + embedding cluster) and a separate reuse bucket for template matches which tend to have much higher reuse. templates are prime candidates for longer TTLs.
[13:50] Priya: excellent. what about warmstart cost — if we warm more sessions, does that increase model warmup token generation?
[14:00] Eli: there's an up-front warming cost: you might produce N tokens to rebuild context. However with prefix reuse and correct prefetch choices you can often amortize that cost across many subsequent requests.
[14:20] James: in our tests we saw a transient 2x token generation for warmstart sequences but then reduced sustained tokens per session by 30%.
[14:35] Marta: okay. next steps from our side: we will run a TTL sweep on staging and capture p95/p50 and token deltas.
[14:45] Priya: timeline — when can you send the annotated export?
[14:50] Samir: i'll send it by Monday the 18th, lena will include knob defaults and the runbook.
[15:05] James: also can we get a short doc on embedding sampling config for drift detection?
[15:15] Lena: yes, i'll include a one-pager on sampling rate, vector size, and similarity thresholds.
[15:30] Tom: on the infra side, minor ask — when you send the export, include memory footprint at 1x, 1.25x, and 1.5x TTL multiplier so we can project capacity.
[15:45] Eli: will do. the sheet will have those columns.
[16:05] Marta: are there any blockers to us running the sweep? secrets, access?
[16:15] James: we can run in staging, we might need a small toggle in the config but nothing blocking.
[16:25] Priya: security asks — send the SOC2 and confirm we can hash prefixes before sending them to Redwood's runtime.
[16:35] Samir: yes, you can hash upstream; we'll confirm the recommended hashing approach in the doc and share SOC2.
[16:50] Martha: (laugh) i said martha but it's marta, sorry.
[16:55] Samir: no worries.
[17:05] Priya: anything on competitors — we briefly evaluated Anthropic's endpoint + in-house cache. why pick Redwood here?
[17:15] Samir: two main things — runtime-level eviction + routing we provide out-of-the-box, and unified tooling to measure token economics. and we have dedicated dev time to tune these heuristics.
[17:40] Priya: cool. james and tom, any last infra concerns?
[17:50] James: only the replica convergence question — we'll test local thermostat first and then try a coordinator if needed.
[18:05] Tom: ok. agree.
[18:15] Samir: quick recap of next steps: we (Redwood) send annotated hit-rate sheet + runbook + SOC2 by 2027-01-18; helmora runs TTL sweep and embedding sample on staging by 2027-01-22; schedule 90-min deep dive week of 2027-01-25.
[18:35] Priya: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[18:40] Samir: thanks all, we'll follow up in email.
[18:45] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings around "thermostat" vs "thermostat" (okay), "KV cache" sometimes transcribed as "KV cahce". Speaker labels mostly accurate but sometimes truncated.
